title: Phase 12: Scale the system and document trade-offs
description: Project: Phase 12: Scale the system and document trade-offs. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: The expense platform is live. Users are submitting expenses, managers are approving them, and finance is running reports. Now you need to handle growth: more users, more receipts, more batch jobs, and lower latency targets. Scaling is not just about adding servers; it is about choosing where to invest engineering time and cloud budget to get the most reliability per dollar.

Scale has two dimensions: vertical and horizontal. Vertical scaling makes a single instance more powerful—larger CPU, more memory. Horizontal scaling adds more instances behind a load balancer. Vertical scaling is simpler but has a hard ceiling. Horizontal scaling is more complex but can grow almost indefinitely.

data.title: Scaling strategies for the expense platform
items: Vertical scaling: upgrade the database to a larger tier when CPU or IOPS saturates
Horizontal scaling: add API instances behind the load balancer when request latency rises
Database read replicas: offload reporting queries to a read replica to reduce primary load
Caching: cache frequent queries and static data in Redis to reduce database round-trips
Queue-based processing: decouple expensive operations into background jobs with autoscaling workers
Database sharding: partition expense data by tenant or date when a single database cannot hold the volume
Cost optimization: use reserved instances for baseline capacity and spot instances for batch workers

terms.definition: Adding more instances to distribute load, also known as scaling out.
Increasing the resources of a single instance, also known as scaling up.
Controlling the number of requests a client can make in a given time window to protect the backend.
A pattern that stops calling a failing service after a threshold of failures, preventing cascading outages.
Splitting a large dataset into smaller, independent pieces called shards, each stored on a separate database instance.
Reducing cloud spend without breaking SLAs through right-sizing, reserved instances, and tiered storage.

data.text: The API layer is the easiest to scale because it is stateless. Add instances behind the load balancer, configure auto-scaling rules based on CPU or request queue depth, and use a health probe to remove unhealthy instances. The challenge is not scaling up; it is ensuring that every layer beneath the API can handle the increased load.

items: Configure auto-scaling with a minimum of two instances and a maximum based on load testing.
Use a health probe path such as /healthz that checks the database and Redis connectivity.
Enable session affinity only if the application cannot store session state externally.
Add a rate limiter to protect the API from abusive clients and sudden traffic spikes.
Use a CDN for static assets such as receipt images and JavaScript bundles.
Monitor the load balancer's request rate and p99 latency to detect saturation early.

data.text: The data layer is usually the hardest to scale because databases are stateful. The expense platform should start with a single managed database, add read replicas for reporting, and only consider sharding when the data volume or write throughput exceeds the capacity of a single instance.

data.text: Cloud costs grow with usage, but they do not have to grow linearly. Right-size instances, use reserved capacity for baseline load, and use spot or preemptible instances for batch workers. Tier storage: hot data on SSD, warm data on standard object storage, and cold data in archive. Every dollar saved on infrastructure is a dollar that can be invested in features.

data.title: Cost optimization tactics
items: Right-size API instances based on actual CPU and memory utilization, not guesswork
Use reserved instances for 24/7 workloads such as the database and API
Use spot instances for the background batch worker, which can tolerate interruption
Compress receipt images before uploading to reduce storage and egress costs
Set lifecycle policies to move old receipts from hot to cool to archive storage
Use a CDN to reduce origin egress for static assets
Enable cost alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the monthly budget

cards.title: Vertical scaling
cards.description: Upgrade a single server to a larger instance type.

cards.title: Horizontal scaling
cards.description: Add more instances behind a load balancer.
cons: Load balancer is a shared dependency

cards.title: Database sharding
cards.description: Partition data across multiple database instances.
pros: Can use cheaper hardware per shard

data.title: Premature scaling is the root of all waste
data.text: Do not shard a database that fits comfortably on a single instance. Do not deploy a global CDN for an app with 500 users. Scale when you have data that shows you need to, not when you imagine you might.

As the system scales, the team structure must scale with it. Conway's Law states that organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure. If you want a scalable system, align teams with bounded contexts: one team owns the expense API, another owns reporting, and a platform team provides shared infrastructure.

items: Map each bounded context to a two-pizza team with full ownership
Create a platform team for CI/CD, observability, and secrets management
Document team boundaries and escalation paths in an architecture wiki
Review team boundaries quarterly and adjust as the product grows

data.text: Every architecture decision has trade-offs. Documenting them is not optional; it is how you preserve institutional knowledge. An Architecture Decision Record captures the context, options, decision, and consequences. When the context changes—such as traffic tripling or a new compliance requirement—the ADR tells future engineers why the system is the way it is.

items.question: How do I know when to scale?
items.answer: Scale when you have data, not hunches. Set SLOs for latency and availability. When you consistently breach the error budget or latency target, use profiling and load testing to identify the bottleneck before scaling.

items.question: What is the difference between scaling and optimizing?
items.answer: Scaling adds resources to handle more load. Optimizing reduces the resources needed per request. A senior engineer optimizes first because it is cheaper, then scales because it is necessary.

items.question: How do I communicate scaling costs to stakeholders?
items.answer: Present the cost per user or transaction. 'Scaling to 100,000 users costs an additional $200 per month in database and compute, but it reduces p99 latency from 800ms to 200ms.' Tie infrastructure decisions to business outcomes.

items.question: What should I document about trade-offs?
items.answer: Document the constraint you were optimizing for, the alternative you rejected, and the measurable outcome. 'We chose eventual consistency for expense approval notifications because strong consistency required a distributed transaction that added 300ms latency and $400 per month in extra infrastructure.'

data.title: Scale the expense platform for 100,000 users
data.description: Using the current architecture, design a scaling plan that handles 100,000 monthly active users with p99 API latency under 200ms and a monthly infrastructure budget of $1,000.
steps: Estimate QPS and storage requirements for 100,000 users
Identify the current bottlenecks using load testing and profiling
Propose scaling changes for each layer: API, database, cache, and worker
Estimate the monthly cost of each scaling option
Document the trade-offs in an Architecture Decision Record
Present the plan to a stakeholder, explaining why each change is necessary
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a scaling plan with cost estimates, a prioritized roadmap, and documented trade-offs that a future team member can understand.

data.title: Summary
points: Scale horizontally for the API layer; scale vertically for the database only when necessary
Use read replicas to offload reporting queries
Decouple expensive work into queues with autoscaling workers
Optimize for cost before optimizing for scale
Document every trade-off in an ADR so future teams understand the context
data.takeaway: Scaling is an engineering conversation with business stakeholders. The best answer is not the most complex architecture; it is the one that meets reliability targets within budget and can evolve as the product grows.
